content: The potato refers to the starchy tuberous crop derived from the perennial plant Solanum tuberosum, which belongs to the Solanaceae family, commonly known as the nightshade family. It is also the term used to describe the plant itself. Potatoes are the most widely cultivated tuber crop globally and rank as the fourth largest food crop in terms of fresh produce, following rice, wheat, and maize (corn). The potato originated in the region of modern-day Peru and subsequently spread from South America to Spain, and later to the rest of the world, following European colonization in the late 1400s and early 1500s. In the town of San Andreas in southern Bolivia, up to 300 varieties of potatoes are showcased annually at the local potato festival. Over time, potatoes became a critical food staple and field crop. For example, they served as a staple food for sailors aboard Spanish ships. After the wreck of the Spanish Armada in 1588, Irish coastal villagers salvaged potatoes and began cultivating them. In 1845, a fungal disease known as Phytophthora infestans (late blight) rapidly spread through impoverished communities in western Ireland, leading to the Great Irish Famine. The local population had become heavily dependent on potatoes, and successive crop failures resulted in widespread death and emigration, primarily to the United States. Many blamed the British government for exacerbating the crisis. Potatoes are strongly associated with regions such as Idaho, Maine, North Dakota, Prince Edward Island, Ireland, Jersey, and Russia due to their significant role in the agricultural economies and histories of these areas. Etymology The English word potato is derived from the Spanish term patata, which ultimately traces back to the Nahuatl word potatl, possibly its original name. The Bulgarian word картоф, as well as the Russian картофель and German Kartoffel, originate from the Italian word tartufoli, named for its resemblance to truffles (tartufo in Italian). Another common name for the potato is ground apple, as seen in French (pomme de terre), Dutch (aardappel), Hebrew (תפוח אדמה), and Austrian German (Erdapfel). In Finnish, the term peruna comes from the old Swedish word jordpäron, meaning earth pear. In 16th-century French, pomme referred to fruit, and pomme de terre literally meant ground fruit, a term that was likely translated into other languages when potatoes were introduced. In Polish, potatoes are called ziemniaki, and in Slovak, zemiak, both derived from the word for ground. In northern Indian languages and Nepali, the potato is known as alu, while in Indonesian, it is called kentang. In China, regional names for potatoes vary, but the most common terms in standard Chinese today are horse-bell yam (马铃薯), earth bean (土豆), and foreign taro (洋芋). Description Potato plants grow close to the ground and produce flowers ranging from yellow to silver, with yellow stamens. Cross-pollination occurs primarily through bumblebees, although self-fertilization is also common. Potatoes can be propagated vegetatively by planting tubers, tuber pieces with at least one or two eyes, or cuttings, a method often used in greenhouses to produce healthy seed tubers. Some commercial potato varieties do not produce seeds at all due to imperfect flowers and are propagated exclusively from tuber pieces, which are referred to as seed potatoes. After flowering, certain potato varieties produce small green fruits resembling green cherry tomatoes, each containing up to 300 true seeds. These seeds can be separated from the fruit by blending them with water, allowing the seeds to sink while the fruit material floats. All new potato varieties are grown from these true seeds or botanical seeds, as opposed to seed tubers. Origin and History Modern botanists agree that the potato originated in the Andes, spanning from Colombia to northern Argentina, with a concentration of genetic diversity in modern-day Peru. The cultivated potatoes in the Andes are not all of the same species. The primary species is Solanum tuberosum ssp. andigena (a tetraploid with 48 chromosomes). Additionally, there are four diploid species (Solanum stenotomum, Solanum phureja, Solanum goniocalyx, and Solanum ajanhuiri), two triploid species (Solanum chaucha and Solanum juzepczukii), and one pentaploid cultivated species (Solanum curtilobum). Andean potatoes are adapted to short-day conditions, while Chilean potatoes are suited to long-day conditions. Evidence suggests that the tetraploid Andean short-day potato was the first to arrive in southern Spain around 1565, from where it spread to the rest of Europe, adapting to European long-day conditions over approximately 200 years. Taxonomists have since divided Solanum tuberosum into two subspecies: tuberosum (adapted to long days) and andigena (adapted to short days). These subspecies differ morphologically, though the distinctions are apparent only to experienced taxonomists. Historical and genetic evidence indicates that the potato reached India shortly after its introduction to Europe, likely brought by the Portuguese. In isolated areas of the Indian Himalayas and Nepal, desi potatoes are still cultivated, closely resembling the short-day-adapted modern Andean potato, Solanum tuberosum ssp. andigena. Globally, there are approximately 5,000 potato varieties, with 3,000 found in the Andes alone, primarily in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, and Colombia. These varieties belong to eight or nine species, depending on the taxonomic classification. In addition to the cultivated varieties, there are about 200 wild species, many of which can be crossbred with cultivated species to transfer pest and disease resistance. However, the varieties commonly found in European, North American, or Asian markets are limited and belong to the species Solanum tuberosum ssp. tuberosum. These are often referred to as Irish potatoes in English-speaking regions due to their association with the Great Irish Famine (1845–1851). Nutrition Potatoes are best known for their carbohydrate content, primarily in the form of starch, with a medium potato containing approximately 26 grams of carbohydrates. A portion of this starch is resistant to enzymatic digestion in the stomach and small intestine, reaching the large intestine intact. Resistant starch provides bulk, protects against colon cancer, improves glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, lowers plasma cholesterol and triglyceride levels, increases satiety, and may reduce fat storage. The amount of resistant starch in potatoes depends on preparation methods; cooking and then cooling potatoes significantly increases resistant starch content. For example, cooked potato starch contains about 7% resistant starch, which increases to approximately 13% upon cooling. Potatoes are also a source of essential vitamins and minerals, including vitamin B6 (10% of the daily value), thiamin, riboflavin, folate, niacin, magnesium, phosphorus, iron, and zinc. The fiber content of a potato with skin (2 grams) is comparable to that of many whole-grain breads, pastas, and cereals. Additionally, potatoes contain phytochemicals such as carotenoids and polyphenols. Contrary to popular belief, the majority of a potato's nutrients are found within the potato itself, not just in the skin. Cooking methods can significantly impact the nutrient availability of potatoes. New and fingerling potatoes contain fewer toxic chemicals and are considered highly nutritious. Peeled, long-stored potatoes have reduced nutritional value but still provide potassium and vitamin B. Potatoes are often classified as high on the glycemic index (GI), leading to their exclusion from low-GI diets. However, the GI can vary depending on the potato variety and preparation method. Toxic Compounds Potatoes contain glycoalkaloids, toxic compounds primarily in the form of solanine and chaconine. These compounds are concentrated just beneath the skin and increase with age and light exposure. Glycoalkaloids can cause symptoms such as headaches, diarrhea, cramps, and, in severe cases, coma and death. However, potato poisoning is rare. Light exposure also causes greening, which can indicate areas of increased toxicity, though greening and glycoalkaloid accumulation can occur independently. Cooking at high temperatures (above 170°C or 340°F) partially destroys glycoalkaloids. Breeders aim to keep solanine levels below 200 mg/kg in commercial varieties, though green potatoes can approach levels of 1,000 mg/kg.
